墨西哥大吉他並非吉他衍生，而是獨立自十六世紀西班牙指甲撥弦低音發展而來。傳統上，: The guitarrón mexicano is not a derivative of the guitar but developed independently from the sixteenth-century Spanish plucked bass played with the fingernails. Traditionally it is the bass and the rhythmic core of the mariachi ensemble, and because it is large it can be played in a small venue without electrical amplification. After the twentieth century Julián Carrillo added frets so that it could play microtones, and used it in Preludio a Colón; Ernie Ball was also inspired by it to bring out a modern acoustic bass. It has entered rock and pop recordings too, with modifications such as a lengthened neck.

Outside traditional settings, Julián Carrillo added frets and turned it into an instrument for microtonal music, used in Preludio a Colón; it also appears on the Mothers of Invention album Freak Out!, on the Eagles' song New Kid in Town, and in performances by the Luminous Orchestra, the Carnival Attraction band, on Talk Talk's album Spirit of Eden, and by Los Lobos.
墨西哥大吉他為大型深腹六弦低音吉他，發聲依靠共鳴箱與拱形背板投射強而深的低音；因: The guitarrón mexicano is a large, deep-bodied six-string bass guitar; it sounds by means of the resonator body and the arched back, which project a strong, deep bass, and because it is large a small venue needs no electrical amplification. The fingerboard has no frets and the strings are thick; the standard tuning is A1, D2, G2, C3, E3, A2, a re-entrant tuning in which the pitch does not rise in one direction along the strings, the sixth string A2 lying below the adjacent E3. Unlike the guitar it is not a guitar derivative but developed independently from the sixteenth-century Spanish plucked bass, and in the mariachi it is responsible for the bass and for driving the rhythm.
墨西哥大吉他（Guitarrón mexicano）是墨西哥的大型六弦原聲貝斯吉: The guitarrón mexicano is a large six-string acoustic bass guitar from Mexico, a chordophone, traditionally used by the mariachi ensemble. It has no frets and carries thick strings, the top three usually nylon and the bottom three wound with metal; the player often plucks two strings at once with the right hand, doubling the bass at the octave, and the instrument is held in front of the body on a strap. Its range is low, and in the mariachi it takes the main rhythmic and bass part, helping the other instruments keep the beat.
